sections.title: How does the Party drink calculator work?
sections.html:
The Party drink calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports beer needed (Results) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (beer?, wine? and hard liquor?); then you type in the party duration, the beer drinkers, the wine drinkers and the hard liquor drinkers.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Party drink calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Beer needed=rounded up, (beer drinkers × party duration)
Wine bottles needed=rounded up, ((1 ÷ 2) × rounded up, ((20 ÷ 43) × wine drinkers))
Hard liquor needed=rounded up, ((1 ÷ 2) × hard liquor drinkers)
Total number of guests=totaldrinks ÷ party duration
Beer needed=rounded up, ((2 ÷ 5) × totaldrinks)
Wine glasses needed=rounded up, ((3 ÷ 5) × totaldrinks − 3 ÷ 5 × rounded up, ((2 ÷ 5) × totaldrinks))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Do you know who will drink what? set to No, Party duration = 30, Beer? set to Yes and Beer drinkers = 10. The calculator returns Beer needed = 600 large bottles, Wine bottles needed = 3, Hard liquor needed = 114 shots and Soft drinks needed = 310.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Beer needed = 600 large bottles, Wine bottles needed = 3, Hard liquor needed = 114 shots and Soft drinks needed = 310 should be roughly the size you expected from Do you know who will drink what? set to No and Party duration = 30.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Beer container sizes, opening in 500 ml
  • Hard liquor, opening in standard shots
  • Beer container sizes, opening in 500 ml

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Party drink calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Scaling a recipe up or down
  • Working out timing so everything finishes together
  • Checking portions before you shop
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the party duration, the beer drinkers and the wine drinkers — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Party drink calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns beer needed (Results), derived from the party duration, the beer drinkers and the wine drinkers. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Party drink calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the party duration, the beer drinkers, the wine drinkers and the hard liquor drinkers, which is 13 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter beer needed (Results) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Beer needed (Results) opens in 500 ml and the chip beside it offers 14 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (5 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Beer needed = 600 large bottles. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Party drink calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
